title: Sister loses five-year legal fight
article: B.C.'s highest court may have finally doused the long-running, corrosive dispute between the Vancouver police department and the sister of dead home invader Jeffrey Michael Berg.
Writing for the three-judge panel, Chief Judge Lance Finch dismissed Julie Berg's appeal of the police complaint hearing decision that her brother's death at the hands of the VPD was justified.
Berg, who has waged a five-year fight to learn the truth about the tragedy, claimed she was denied the right to fully participate in the hearing, that it was unfair and its conclusions wrong.
But Finch tossed her arguments and said there was no reason for the court to interfere with the police complaint ruling.
He said her right to participate in the hearing was circumscribed by law and there was nothing wrong with that.

The province's high bench said complainants' participation was expressly limited "to the making of oral or written submissions after all the evidence is called" and they had "no right to lead evidence or cross-examine witnesses."
"While complainants may volunteer to participate in the hearing, their participation is not required," Finch wrote in the unanimous judgment handed down Friday.
"Under the Police Act, it is commission counsel, not the complainant, who is responsible for presenting the case to the adjudicator."
Berg's secondary plea that she lacked funding to adequately participate in the hearing and required state support also fell on deaf ears.
Supported by colleagues Anne Rowles and Kenneth Mackenzie, Justice Finch said government support is a purely discretionary matter up to Victoria.

"In my view, the adjudicator's decision not to recommend funding was a matter within his complete discretion and Ms. Berg had no right to public funds to pay for legal counsel, or transcripts of the public hearing," he wrote.

This was an important ruling because Berg was challenging the complaints process established by the 1998 police act -- the legislative response to now-attorney-general, then-Justice Wally Oppal's 1994 report Closing the Gap: Policing and Community.

As a result, both the B.C. Civil Liberties Association and the B.C. Association of Municipal Chiefs of Police intervened to give the court their points of view -- respectively pro and con Berg's position.
Although Julie won much sympathy from the media and public throughout the ordeal, her brother was an absolute loser involved in violent robberies and brutal marijuana rip-offs.
On Oct. 22, 2000, the facts say, Const. David Bruce-Thomas confronted Berg fleeing a home invasion in an alley of the 4800- block Slocan.
According to evidence presented at the hearing, Berg went to the house expecting to find a marijuana-growing operation.
He and an accomplice battered down the door. Berg, who wore a black mask, brandished a replica handgun.
The father escaped with two children and called 911.
Berg was collared moments later as he fled.
He died in hospital two days later from a ruptured artery in his neck inflicted during his arrest.

"The respondent officer testified that he kicked Mr. Berg in the crotch area, karate kicked him in the midsection, and that he recalled a third kick but could not say if that kick landed," Justice Finch noted. "He testified that the next thing he recalled was being on the ground on top of Mr. Berg."
Two independent eyewitnesses also testified, the judge added:

"Sari Fujikawa testified that the respondent officer hit Mr. Berg with a gun and then kicked him twice while he was on the ground. The second eyewitness Mr. Wu testified that the respondent officer kicked the man's knee and then handcuffed him and proceeded to kick him several times while he was on the ground handcuffed."
Steve Silver, a former member of the VPD, testified that he saw Bruce-Thomas kick Berg one or two times in the upper thigh region and "one of those kicks may have hit the testicle area."
Julie filed her initial complaint a month after the incident.
The VPD conducted an internal investigation that was suspended for nearly a year pending a review by regional Crown counsel.
In December 2002, Crown counsel decided criminal charges against Bruce-Thomas were not warranted.
Within days, the department announced the results of its investigation -- disciplinary measures were not warranted.
Upon review, the police complaint commissioner determined that the VPD investigation was insufficient and the disciplinary decision also flawed.
As a result, on June 24, 2003, the commissioner ordered a public hearing.
Fifteen months ago, Berg got a decision. She was apoplectic.

While noting conflicting evidence, the complaint commissioner found Bruce-Thomas "had a reasonable belief in the facts that persuaded him to use the force he did and to deliver the blows and kicks that he did."
After four years of acrimonious scrapping, the VPD was cleared, allowing Police Chief Jamie Graham to throw back some of the mud.

He felt Julie Berg's fight was a campaign of "lies and defamations" and accused her of whitewashing her brother's unsavoury life. Had she gone to police, Graham said, "this entire tragic incident may have been avoided."
I always thought that was rather bitter bile.
Berg responded by launching her complaints about the process.
She might not like it, the court said, still she was treated fairly.
"The legislature has determined that complainants have a role to play, but it is a defined and limited role," Finch concluded.
